This chapter covers passing, yielding, emergency vehicles, school buses, signals, turns and roundabouts. Before any of those details, this first lesson sets out the foundation. You will learn what the guide calls a motorist's highest duty, what right-of-way law really says and why it never hands anyone the right to go first, where right-of-way rules apply, who is allowed to make traffic rules, and the fines that apply in work zones. Keep these principles in mind, because every specific rule later in the chapter builds on them.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-R19"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The highest duty","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Careful, prudent driving.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]},{"text":"Safe speed and manner.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]},{"text":"Protect everyone on the road.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"The guide says a motorist's highest duty is careful, prudent driving. That means choosing a speed and a manner of driving that keep the road safe for pedestrians, cyclists and other drivers, as well as for yourself. Notice that the duty is not only about obeying signs. A driver can follow every posted rule and still drive carelessly, for example by going too fast for the conditions. The highest duty asks you to think about everyone sharing the road. Many drivers talk about having the right-of-way, as if the law gave them a right to go first. The guide says right-of-way law only says who must yield. It never gives any driver the right-of-way. So even when another driver should have yielded to you, you must still do everything possible to avoid striking a pedestrian or a vehicle, no matter the circumstances. On a test, any answer that says you may go ahead because you had the right-of-way, even if a crash may follow, is wrong. Safety always comes first.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Where the rules apply","fact_ids":["sec04-R10","sec04-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Where road users are likely to meet.","fact_ids":["sec04-R10","sec04-F02"]},{"text":"Where no signs or signals control.","fact_ids":["sec04-R10","sec04-F02"]},{"text":"They decide who goes and who waits.","fact_ids":["sec04-R10","sec04-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Right-of-way rules exist for places where vehicles or pedestrians are likely to meet and no signs or signals control traffic. In those places, the rules say who goes first and who waits. Where a signal or a sign does control traffic, you follow it, and where nothing controls traffic, the right-of-way rules fill the gap. Later lessons give the specific rules for left turns, four-way stops, uncontrolled intersections, driveways and roundabouts. Each of those is simply an answer to the same question: when two road users meet, which one must wait.","fact_ids":["sec04-R10","sec04-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Rules and work zones","fact_ids":["sec04-R19","sec04-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Cities, counties and the state set rules.","fact_ids":["sec04-R19","sec04-F03"]},{"text":"Local rules can add limits.","fact_ids":["sec04-R19","sec04-F03"]},{"text":"Work zone fines start at two hundred fifty dollars.","fact_ids":["sec04-R19","sec04-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Traffic rules come from more than one place. Cities, counties and the state can all set traffic rules, and you must obey each. Local rules may set speed limits, one-way streets and stop signs, keep commercial vehicles off certain streets, control parking and turns, require signals, brake lights and horns, or ban sound-producing warning devices. Work zones get special attention: speeding or passing in a construction or work zone on Missouri state roads can bring a fine of at least two hundred fifty dollars for a first offense, and at least three hundred dollars for any later offense, on top of other fines.","fact_ids":["sec04-R19","sec04-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the right-of-way idea","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"He had the right-of-way.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F01"]},{"text":"Is the crash not his concern?","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: after a crash, a driver insists he had the right-of-way, so what happened was not his concern. Every driver must do everything possible to avoid striking a pedestrian or another vehicle, no matter the circumstances. So even if the other driver should have yielded, he still had a duty to avoid the crash if he could. That duty comes from the highest duty of careful, prudent driving.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Foundation recap","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-R10","sec04-R19","sec04-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Careful, prudent driving first.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-R10","sec04-R19","sec04-F03"]},{"text":"Yield rules name who waits.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-R10","sec04-R19","sec04-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close this first lesson: your highest duty is careful, prudent driving that keeps the road safe for everyone. Right-of-way rules apply where road users meet without signs or signals. Cities, counties and the state all set rules you must obey, and work zone speeding or passing on state roads brings fines of at least two hundred fifty dollars. never the shoulder.","fact_ids":["sec04-R01","sec04-F07"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"On a highway outside a city, what does the pavement need before you may pass on the right?","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F06"]},"answer":{"text":"Clear pavement wide enough and marked for four or more lanes.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06","sec04-R03"]},"rationale":{"text":"Outside a city the highway needs four or more marked lanes, while a city street needs room for two or more lines each way.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F05"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"When and where to pass","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Passing people on foot and bikes.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F09"]},{"text":"Passing on the right.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F09"]},{"text":"No-passing places.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers passing. Two of those places share the same distance, so you will learn to keep them together. You will also see which conditions make passing more dangerous in general. Passing brings you close to oncoming traffic or beside other vehicles, so these rules matter for your safety and for everyone near you.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Passing people and bikes","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Same care as passing a car.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R11"]},{"text":"Slow and wait for a safe chance.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Pass a pedestrian or a cyclist with the same care you would use to pass a motor vehicle. Waiting a few moments for a clear stretch is always better than squeezing past. Treat them as traffic that deserves room, not as obstacles to rush around. The guide also notes that intersections and two-lane roads add to the danger of any pass.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Passing on the right","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Vehicle ahead turning left.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07"]},{"text":"Wide city street or one-way street.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07"]},{"text":"Four-lane highway outside a city.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Passing on the right is allowed only in certain situations. You may pass on the right when the vehicle ahead is turning left or about to, or on a city street with clear pavement wide enough for two or more lines of vehicles each way. It is also allowed on a one-way street, or on a highway outside a city with clear pavement wide enough and marked for four or more lanes. Do not drive left of center within one hundred feet of or at an intersection or railroad grade crossing, or anywhere a solid yellow line is present. So whenever a question asks how close you may drive left of center to a bridge, tunnel, intersection or crossing, the distance is the same. Do not confuse it with other figures in the chapter, such as the five hundred feet that appears in the school bus and turn-lane rules later on.","fact_ids":["sec04-R01","sec04-F09","sec04-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the highway rule","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F06","sec04-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Highway outside a city.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F06","sec04-F05"]},{"text":"When may you pass on the right?","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F06","sec04-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are on a highway outside a city and want to pass a slower car on the right. Pass on the right only when the vehicle ahead is turning left, on a wide city street, on a one-way street, or on a highway marked for four or more lanes, and never on the shoulder. Do not move left near a blind hill crest or curve, within one hundred feet of a bridge, viaduct or tunnel with a blocked view, within one hundred feet of an intersection or railroad crossing, or where a solid yellow line is present. Three of these rules are easy to confuse, so near the end the lesson puts them side by side. Remember from the last lesson that these rules only say who must yield; they never give anyone a right to go first if a crash could follow.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11","sec04-F13","sec04-F16"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Pedestrians and driveways","fact_ids":["sec04-F11","sec04-F14"]},"lines":[{"text":"Yield to legal pedestrian crossings.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11","sec04-F14"]},{"text":"Driveway or alley: yield to walkers.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11","sec04-F14"]},{"text":"Then yield to main-road traffic.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11","sec04-F14"]}],"narration":{"text":"Drivers yield as needed to avoid hitting pedestrians crossing legally. So the vehicle on your right does not get priority at a roundabout; the vehicles already in the circle do. Keep the exception in mind: the yield-to-the-right rule is for plain uncontrolled intersections, and roundabouts are specifically left out of it.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F16"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Three intersection rules","fact_ids":["sec04-R07","sec04-F13","sec04-F15","sec04-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"Four-way stop: arrival order.","fact_ids":["sec04-R07","sec04-F13","sec04-F15","sec04-F16"]},{"text":"Uncontrolled: vehicle on the right.","fact_ids":["sec04-R07","sec04-F13","sec04-F15","sec04-F16"]},{"text":"Roundabout: traffic in the circle.","fact_ids":["sec04-R07","sec04-F13","sec04-F15","sec04-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Three intersection types each have their own priority rule, and test questions often mix them up. A four-way stop goes by arrival order: the first driver to stop goes first.
